claim: The dorsal vagal complex (DVC) is a region in the brainstem comprised of an intricate network of specialized cells responsible for sensing and propagating many appetite-related cues.
source: The dorsal vagal complex (DVC) is a region in the brainstem comprised of an intricate network of specialized cells responsible for sensing and propagating many appetite-related cues.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the DVC's anatomical location and function in appetite regulation.

claim: A multi-species DVC cell atlas was generated using single-nuclei RNA-sequencing, by curating and harmonizing mouse and rat data, which includes >180,000 cells and 123 cell identities at 5 granularities of cellular resolution.
source: We generated a multi-species DVC cell atlas using single-nuclei RNA-sequencing, by curating and harmonizing mouse and rat data, which includes >180,000 cells and 123 cell identities at 5 granularities of cellular resolution.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the data presented in the manuscript describing the atlas construction and cell counts.

claim: Kcnj3 is expressed in Ca+-permeable astrocytes in the DVC.
source: We report unique DVC features such as Kcnj3 expression in Ca+-permeable astrocytes
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing Kcnj3 expression patterns in astrocytes.

claim: There are new cell populations of neurons co-expressing Th and Cck in the DVC.
source: as well as new cell populations like neurons co-expressing Th and Cck
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data and in situ hybridization showing co-expression.

claim: A leptin receptor-expressing neuron population exists in the rat area postrema which is marked by expression of the progenitor marker, Pdgfra.
source: and a leptin receptor-expressing neuron population in the rat area postrema which is marked by expression of the progenitor marker, Pdgfra.
evidence: This is supported by snRNA-seq data and immunofluorescence showing Pdgfra and HuC/D co-expression in rat AP.

claim: The DVC acts as a key nexus point for metabolic signals, evidenced by the dense expression of many relevant hormone receptors (Ludwig et al., 2021).
source: Within the brainstem, the dorsal vagal complex (DVC), comprising the area postrema (AP), nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, acts as a key nexus point for metabolic signals, evidenced by the dense expression of many relevant hormone receptors (Ludwig et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The DVC serves as the primary site of gut-based signals via vagal afferents (Bai et al., 2019; Han et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2016).
source: Separately, the DVC also serves as the primary site of gut-based signals via vagal afferents (Bai et al., 2019; Han et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The DVC was long considered a site promoting meal termination (Schwartz, 2006).
source: Functionally, the DVC was long considered a site promoting meal termination (Schwartz, 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Growing evidence suggests the DVC also controls long-term energy balance (Cheng et al., 2021).
source: but growing evidence suggests it also controls long-term energy balance (Cheng et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: GLP1R expression is particularly enriched in DVC neurons (Adams et al., 2018).
source: While expressed across the central nervous system, GLP1R expression is particularly enriched in DVC neurons (Adams et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The DVC mediates many of the effects of GLP1R agonists (Huang et al., 2024).
source: and it is the DVC that mediates many of the effects of GLP1R agonists (Huang et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: An emerging strategy for treating cancer cachexia is inhibiting growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) signaling in the DVC by blocking the action of GFRAL (Medic et al., 2022).
source: Separately, an emerging strategy for treating cancer cachexia is inhibiting growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) signaling in the DVC by blocking the action of GDNF Family Receptor Alpha Like (GFRAL) (Medic et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: GFRAL is the receptor for GDF15 (Yang et al., 2017).
source: the receptor for GDF15 (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Cholecystokinin and monoamine-expressing cells, demarcated by tyrosine hydroxylase (Th) expression, were previously shown to be non-overlapping cell populations with unique roles in appetite suppression (Roman et al., 2016).
source: For instance, the cholecystokinin and monoamine-expressing cells, demarcated by tyrosine hydroxylase (Th) expression, were previously shown to be non-overlapping cell populations with unique roles in appetite suppression (Roman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Single-cell mRNA sequencing approaches have revealed the complexity of the mouse DVC, comprised of dozens of transcriptionally distinct cell types (Ludwig et al., 2021; Dowsett et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
source: Such studies focusing on the mouse have revealed the complexity of the mouse DVC, comprised of dozens of transcriptionally distinct cell types (Ludwig et al., 2021; Dowsett et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: From the CellRanger pre-processing pipeline (Zheng et al., 2017), 110,167 cells were obtained of which 99,740 were retained after processing.
source: From the CellRanger pre-processing pipeline (Zheng et al., 2017), we obtained 110,167 cells of which 99,740 were retained after processing.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the sequencing pipeline and citation to the CellRanger method.

claim: Cell identities were initially mapped to 5 databases from different brain regions and then curated manually using 473 cell identity markers.
source: Cell identities were initially mapped to 5 databases from different brain regions and then curated manually using 473 cell identity markers (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the described methodology and reference to supplementary data.

claim: Among the 10 neuronal cell classes identified at layer-2 resolution, two major groups were found which were called 'magnaclass 1' and 'magnaclass 2'.
source: Among the 10 neuronal cell classes identified at layer-2 resolution, we found two major groups which we called 'magnaclass 1' and 'magnaclass 2' (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Magnaclass 1 neurons predominately express genes required for inhibitory neurotransmission (e.g. Gad1 and Gad2).
source: Magnaclass 1 neurons predominately express genes required for inhibitory neurotransmission (e.g. Gad1 and Gad2)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in figures.

claim: Magnaclass 2 neurons express mostly excitatory transcripts (e.g. the glutamate transporter VGLUT2).
source: whereas magnaclass 2 neurons express mostly excitatory transcripts (e.g. the glutamate transporter VGLUT2)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in figures.

claim: The Golli-class neurons express multiple myelin-associated genes such as Mag and Mog (Landry et al., 1996; Lutz et al., 2014; Cheli et al., 2016) normally expressed by oligodendrocytes.
source: Golli-class neurons express multiple myelin-associated genes such as Mag and Mog (Landry et al., 1996; Lutz et al., 2014; Cheli et al., 2016) normally expressed by oligodendrocytes (Figure 1D; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to prior literature on these genes.

claim: A class of neurons was identified with genes normally upregulated in astrocytes (e.g. Slc6a11) and related to clearance and uptake of glutamate, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), Ca+, and bicarbonate (Melone et al., 2014; Theparambil et al., 2020), which was named 'pH-related class'.
source: Additionally, we identified a class of neurons with genes normally upregulated in astrocytes (e.g. Slc6a11) and related to clearance and uptake of glutamate, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), Ca+, and bicarbonate (Melone et al., 2014; Theparambil et al., 2020), which we named 'pH-related class' (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to prior literature on gene function.

claim: Expression of Cdk8 is largely absent from the DVC but is enriched within the DVC-adjacent hypoglossal nucleus, suggesting corelautus-class neurons are hypoglossal neurons.
source: Expression of Cdk8 is largely absent from the DVC but is enriched within the DVC-adjacent hypoglossal nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting these cells are hypoglossal neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from spatial expression patterns shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pvalb is highly expressed in the neighboring cuneate nucleus, suggesting the Lhx2-class may belong to this anatomically adjacent area which was captured in the dissection.
source: As Pvalb is highly expressed in the neighboring cuneate nucleus (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we posit this class may belong to this anatomically adjacent area which was captured in our dissection.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from spatial expression patterns and speculation about cell origin.

claim: DVC-specific neuronal programs exist that are not found in the hypothalamus.
source: When interrogating snRNA-seq data from the hypothalamus (Steuernagel et al., 2022; Figure 1—figure supplement 3), another brain site important for energy balance, we could not find clusters sharing all markers with our neuronal classes, indicating DVC-specific neuronal programs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on comparative analysis with hypothalamic data and inference about DVC specificity.

claim: Two major groups of astrocytes were differentiated, including a group with high expression of the inwardly rectifying GIRK1 (Kcnj3) channel (Kubo et al., 1993) and lack of expression of the AMPAr subunit GluA2 (Gria2), rendering them K+/Na+/Ca+-permeable (Burnashev et al., 1992; Geiger et al., 1995).
source: Differential expression in synapse-related factors revealed a group of astrocytes with high expression of the inwardly rectifying GIRK1 (Kcnj3) channel (Kubo et al., 1993) and lack of expression of the AMPAr subunit GluA2 (Gria2), additionally rendering them K+/Na+/Ca+-permeable (Burnashev et al., 1992; Geiger et al., 1995; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to prior literature on channel properties.

claim: Kcnj3+; Gria2- astrocytes are specific to the DVC and not found in the hypothalamus, forebrain, cortex, or hippocampus (Steuernagel et al., 2022; Batiuk et al., 2020; Jessa et al., 2019).
source: We speculate these astrocytes are specific to the DVC as we could not find Kcnj3+; Gria2- astrocytes in the hypothalamus, forebrain, cortex, or hippocampus (Steuernagel et al., 2022; Batiuk et al., 2020; Jessa et al., 2019; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on comparative analysis with other brain regions and speculation about DVC specificity.

claim: A spectrum of DVC mature oligodendrocytes was distinguished, including a group resembling the intermediate oligodendrocytes described in other brain sites that decrease in number with age (Marques et al., 2016; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018).
source: In addition, we distinguished a spectrum of DVC mature oligodendrocytes, including a group resembling the intermediate oligodendrocytes described in the other brain sites that decrease in number with age (Marques et al., 2016; Sathyamurthy et al., 2018; Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to prior literature on oligodendrocyte maturation.

claim: The gradient of expression of markers including Fyn, Opalin, and Anln in oligodendrocytes does not respond to a developmental trajectory.
source: This gradient of expression of markers including Fyn, Opalin, and Anln in oligodendrocytes (Figure 2C), does not respond to a developmental trajectory (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by trajectory analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Two fibroblast subtypes were distinguished, one of which expresses high Stk39 previously described in fibroblast stress-response (Kasai et al., 2022) and was termed 's-fibroblasts' for stress-associated fibroblasts.
source: One of these subtypes expresses high Stk39 previously described in fibroblast stress-response (Kasai et al., 2022) and so was termed 's-fibroblasts' for stress-associated fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citation to prior literature on Stk39 function.

claim: S-fibroblasts were not detected in the hypothalamus.
source: which we failed to detect in the hypothalamus (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on comparative analysis with hypothalamic data.

claim: DVC microglial cells are in a basal state with minimal levels of activation genes Cxcl10, Cd5, Cxcl9, and Zbp1 (DePaula-Silva et al., 2019).
source: Additionally, we excluded the possibility of monocytes in our microglial data (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which had no evidence of microglial activation as we mapped minimal levels of the activation genes Cxcl10, Cd5, Cxcl9, and Zbp1 (DePaula-Silva et al., 2019) therefore , we posit that our DVC microglial cells are in a basal state (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression analysis and inference about activation state, with citation to prior literature on activation markers.

claim: A group of microglia expressing oligodendrocyte markers was identified, resembling a subpopulation of hippocampal microglia in an Alzheimer's disease model which is disease-protective and synaptic-function-supporting (Koutsodendris et al., 2023), and a cortical/subcortical phagocytic subpopulation in a multiple sclerosis model (Schirmer et al., 2019).
source: We have identified a group of microglia expressing oligodendrocyte markers and resembling a subpopulation of hippocampal microglia in an Alzheimer's disease model which is disease-protective and synaptic-function-supporting (Koutsodendris et al., 2023), and a cortical/subcortical phagocytic subpopulation in a multiple sclerosis model (Schirmer et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression patterns and citations to prior literature on similar microglial populations.

claim: A second group of microglia expresses Ndrg2 and receptors for GABA and glutamate which have been related to microglia that may induce neuronal damage (Creus-Muncunill et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2016).
source: A second group expresses Ndrg2 and receptors for GABA and glutamate which have been related to microglia that may induce neuronal damage (Creus-Muncunill et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2016; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression patterns and citations to prior literature on microglial function.

claim: The monoamine class was split into four layer-3 cell identities (i.e. M0, M1, M2, and M3) with specific cell markers.
source: Additionally, we split the monoamine class into four layer-3 cell identities (i.e. M0, M1, M2, and M3) with specific cell markers (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: M0 and M1 neurons express genes for enzymes synthesizing norepinephrine and serotonin, but M0 expresses minimal levels of the transporter VMAT2 (Slc18a2).
source: M0 and M1 neurons express genes for enzymes synthesizing norepinephrine and serotonin, but M0 expresses minimal levels of the transporter VMAT2 (Slc18a2) (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: M2 and M3 neurons are considered monoamine modulators as they seem to synthesize trace amines due to the low proportion of cells expressing Th and Tph2.
source: Due to the low proportion of cells expressing Th and Tph2 in M2 and M3 neurons, we consider them monoamine modulators as they seem to synthesize trace amines (Figure 3C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns.

claim: The receptor for GDF15, GFRAL, is expressed heavily by a subset of M0 neurons, some of which co-express the calcium sensing receptor (Casr) gene.
source: Of note, the receptor for GDF15, GFRAL, is expressed heavily by a subset of M0 neurons, some of which co-express the calcium sensing receptor (Casr) gene (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: GLP1 neurons express high levels of both the prolactin and leptin receptors (Cheng et al., 2020b).
source: which also expresses high levels of both the prolactin and leptin receptors (Cheng et al., 2020b; Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citation to prior literature.

claim: GLP1 neurons have the highest proportion of DVC neuronal co-expression of glutamate- and GABA-related genes, mainly Gad2 with considerably lower expression of Slc32a1.
source: Additionally, these cells have the highest proportion of DVC neuronal co-expression of glutamate- and GABA-related genes (Figure 3F); mainly Gad2 with considerably lower expression of Slc32a1.
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: >10% of the Th-expressing neurons also express Cck in the snRNA-seq data.
source: While the Cck- and Th-expressing DVC neurons are considered to be non-overlapping cell types with distinct physiologies (Roman et al., 2016; Roman et al., 2017), we quantified >10% of the Th-expressing neurons also expressing Cck in our snRNA-seq data.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of co-expression in snRNA-seq data.

claim: Co-expression of Th and Cck was confirmed by in situ hybridization.
source: We further confirmed co-expression of Th and Cck results by in situ hybridization (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The majority of Th/Cck overlap occurs in cells belonging to the COE-Atp10a and monoamine class (i.e. M0, M3) cell identities.
source: The majority of this overlap occurs in cells belonging to the COE-Atp10a and monoamine class (i.e. M0, M3) cell identities (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of co-expression patterns shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The murine hierarchy has a fourth layer of cellular resolution as some of Ludwig identities, mainly neurons, are subgroups of the study's cell identities.
source: The resultant murine hierarchy has a fourth layer of cellular resolution as some of Ludwig identities, mainly neurons, are subgroups of our cell identities (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the hierarchical integration analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 95% of cells from the Dowsett dataset were successfully labeled at high resolution (i.e. layer-3 or -4 of cell identity granularity) using the learned model.
source: Using this approach, we were able to successfully label 95% of these cells at high resolution (i.e. layer-3 or -4 of cell identity granularity); further validating our combined DVC labels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the label transfer analysis results.

claim: A de novo ad libitum-fed rat dataset was generated with 12,167 cells.
source: To identify rat DVC cell clusters and subclusters and contrast these with the mouse DVC atlas, we generated a de novo ad libitum-fed rat dataset (cells n = 12,167) (Figure 6A)
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data from rat sequencing.

claim: 52 DVC rat identities were obtained at high cellular resolution.
source: After manual curation at three granularities (Figure 6B, C; Supplementary file 3), we obtained 52 DVC rat identities at high cellular resolution (Figure 6C)
evidence: This claim is supported by the rat data analysis.

claim: 10 layer-3 neuronal identities were established in rat that were not previously found in the murine data.
source: We established 10 layer-3 neuronal identities not previously found in the murine data (Figure 6C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of rat and mouse data.

claim: Two new layer-2 classes were created in rat: immunity-related neurons and Pdgfra neurons (ortus-akin class).
source: Notably, two of those did not belong to any of the existing murine neuronal classes (i.e. layer-2 of cellular granularity); therefore, we created two new layer-2 classes (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the rat data analysis showing novel cell classes.

claim: Immunity-related neurons have high Csf1r expression, as well as cystatin C and Inpp5d which are commonly associated with immunity-related processes in microglia and with immunomodulation in cancer (Chou et al., 2023; Kleeman et al., 2023).
source: One of these, the immunity-related neurons, has high Csf1r expression, as well as cystatin C and Inpp5d which are commonly associated with immunity-related processes in microglia and with immunomodulation in cancer (Chou et al., 2023; Kleeman et al., 2023; Figure 7; Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citations to prior literature on gene function.

claim: Pdgfra neurons express Pdgfra, Arhgap31, and Itga9, known markers for progenitor cells (Kang et al., 2010).
source: These neurons express Pdgfra, Arhgap31, and Itga9, known markers for progenitor cells for which we named this cell class 'ortus-akin' (Latin: 'origin') because they are similar to cells giving origin to other cells (Kang et al., 2010; Figure 7A; Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data and citation to prior literature on progenitor markers.

claim: Pdgfra neurons not only expressed Pdgfra, but also other OPC signature genes.
source: Interestingly, this neuronal class not only expressed Pdgfra, but also other OPC signature genes (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A subset (~15%) of both immunity-akin and ortus-akin neurons express detectable Gfral mRNA.
source: Mapping the expression levels of metabolic-associated receptors revealed that a subset (~15%) of both immunity-akin and ortus-akin express detectable Gfral mRNA
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis.

claim: Within the mouse, PDGFRA-immunoreactivity (IR) was found in two morphologically distinct cells; matching OPC and blood vessel-associated fibroblast morphologies.
source: Within the mouse, we found PDGFRA-immunoreactivity (IR) in the two morphologically distinct cells; matching OPC and blood vessel-associated fibroblast morphologies (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Within the rat, PDGFRA-IR was identified in cells with three morphologies, one of which resembled neurons with an enlarged cell body and protruding cellular processes.
source: However, within the rat, we identified PDGFRA-IR in cells with three morphologies, one of which resembled neurons with an enlarged cell body and protruding cellular processes (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Several PDGFRA and HuC/D copositive cells were noted in the rat, confirming that a PDGFRA-expressing neural class exists in the rat DVC and localizing these cells to the AP.
source: To determine if these PDGFRA-IR cells were neurons, we co-stained with the neural marker, HuC/D, and noted several PDGFRA and HuC/D copositive cells (Figure 7D), confirming our sequencing data that a PDGFRA-expressing neural class exists in the rat DVC and localizing these cells to the AP.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence co-staining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The final rodent hierarchy has 123 labels, of which 99 are high resolution according to cellular granularity (i.e. layers 3–5).
source: The final hierarchy has 123 labels, of which 99 are high resolution according to our cellular granularity (i.e. layers 3–5) (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the final integrated atlas shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Hcrt and Agrp mRNA were found in neurons in the dataset.
source: Surprisingly, we found Hcrt and Agrp mRNA in neurons in our dataset (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by snRNA-seq data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: In-situ hybridizations failed to observe Hcrt and Agrp signal within the DVC, although both were readily detectable in the hypothalamus.
source: We then performed in-situ hybridizations for these transcripts in both the mouse hypothalamus and DVC. While both Hcrt and Agrp were readily detectable in the hypothalamus, we failed to observe signal within the DVC (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Most sequenced reads from Hcrt and Agrp mapped to intronic and non-coding regions of these genes.
source: Since we also found expression of Hcrt and Agrp in neurons of the Dowsett and Ludwig datasets (Ludwig et al., 2021; Dowsett et al., 2021; Figure 8—figure supplement 2), we then mapped the sequenced reads from these transcripts and confirmed that most of them mapped to intronic and non-coding regions of these genes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by read mapping analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rat DVC dataset was pre-processed excluding introns from the reads mapping, and the Hcrt and Agrp expression levels observed are minimal.
source: Furthermore, our rat DVC dataset was pre-processed excluding introns from the reads mapping, and the Hcrt and Agrp expression levels observed are minimal (Figure 8—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the rat dataset shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: DVC cells do not produce HCRT or AGRP neuropeptides.
source: These data explain the absence of signal from our in situ hybridizations and suggest DVC cells do not produce HCRT or AGRP neuropeptides.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the combined in situ and sequencing data.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed widespread transcriptional changes across nearly every neural cell identity in response to meal consumption, with exceptions being corelautus, Golli-class, and pH classes.
source: This analysis revealed widespread transcriptional changes across nearly every neural cell identity, the exceptions being corelautus, Golli-class, and pH classes (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The size of the transcriptional changes in response to refeeding was relatively small, with approximately 90% of the differentially expressed genes having increases or decreases between 0.5 and 1.0 log2 fold-change.
source: Additionally, the size of the transcriptional changes was relatively small, with approximately 90% of the differentially expressed genes having increases or decreases between 0.5 and 1.0 log2 fold-change (FC), with only ~10% of the gene changes being ≥1 log2FC between conditions (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of fold-changes from differential expression analysis.

claim: Magnaclasses 1 and 2 showed the greatest number of differentially expressed genes following refeeding for both comparisons refed versus fasting and refed versus ad libitum food access.
source: Of the responding neurons, magnaclasses 1 and 2, which represent large populations of predominately inhibitory and excitatory neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showed the greatest number of differentially expressed genes following refeeding for both comparisons refed versus fasting and refed versus ad libitum food access (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Despite being in transcriptionally distinct classes, meal consumption altered many of the same genes in magnaclasses 1 and 2.
source: Intriguingly, despite being in transcriptionally distinct classes, we found meal consumption altered many of the same genes (Figure 9B–D)
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figures 9B-D.

claim: Magnaclasses 1 and 2 may be receiving similar postprandial signals which are propagated via these cells in unique manners, supported by their similar receptor expression profile.
source: suggesting these cells may be receiving similar postprandial signals which are propagated via these cells in unique manners. This is supported by the similar receptor expression profile of magnaclasses 1 and 2 (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene expression patterns and receptor profiles.

claim: Cckbr is upregulated in magnaclass 2 and downregulated in magnaclass 1 in refeeding when compared with ad libitum fed mice.
source: One notable exception is Cckbr, which is upregulated in magnaclass 2 and downregulated in magnaclass 1 in refeeding when compared with ad libitum fed mice (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis.

claim: Oligodendrocytes contained the highest number of differentially expressed genes in refeeding.
source: We also note that oligodendrocytes contained the highest number of differentially expressed genes in refeeding (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: DVC-specific astrocytes may have specialized functions in regulating blood–brain barrier permeability.
source: As astrocytes have well-established roles in maintaining the blood–brain barrier function (Cabezas et al., 2014), and the pattern of GFAP in the DVC is largely restricted to the boundary separating the AP and NTS, it is possible these DVC-specific astrocytes have specialized functions in regulating blood–brain barrier permeability.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from spatial expression patterns and known astrocyte functions.

claim: The discrepancy between snRNA-seq and immunofluorescent detection of Cck/Th co-expression may be due to detection methods.
source: We believe the discrepancy may be due to detection methods as these cells were initially defined as non-overlapping using immunofluorescent detection of TH protein and a Cck genetic reporter (Roman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about methodological differences.

claim: Dual Cck/Th positive neurons likely mediate aversive anorexia as some Th-expressing AP neurons also express Gfral and Casr, both having potently aversive ligands (e.g. GDF15, deoxynivalenol) (Yang et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2023).
source: While no functional characterization of Cck and Th neurons of the AP has been performed, we posit that as some Th-expressing AP neurons also express Gfral and Casr; both having potently aversive ligands (e.g. GDF15, deoxynivalenol) (Yang et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2023); they are likely to mediate aversive anorexia.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from gene expression patterns and citations about ligand properties.

claim: It is possible that PDGFRA+/HuCD+ cells in the AP represent a transient stage of PDGFRA+ OPCs differentiating into neurons.
source: Since it was previously demonstrated that OPCs can give rise to neurons in the adult brain (Robins et al., 2013) and there is evidence of neurogenesis in the AP following amylin administration in rats (Liberini et al., 2016a), it is possible that these PDGFRA+/HuCD+ cells in the AP represent a transient stage of PDGFRA+ OPCs differentiating into neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation from current findings and citations to prior literature on OPC differentiation and AP neurogenesis.

claim: One explanation for the species discrepancy in Lepr expression between mice and rats is the absence of the ortus class neurons in mice.
source: We believe one explanation for this species discrepancy in Lepr expression is the absence of the ortus class neurons in mice.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the cause of species differences.

claim: The DVC was isolated from 30 adult C57BL/6J mice and subjected to 10X Genomics-based snRNA barcoding and sequencing.
source: To generate a de novo snRNA-seq atlas of the mouse DVC, we isolated the DVC from 30 adult C57BL/6J mice and subjected them to 10X Genomics-based snRNA barcoding and sequencing (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Mice were either fasted overnight (n = 5), fasted overnight and then refed 2 hr prior to euthanasia (n = 10), fed ad libitum (n = 5), injected with LiCl (n = 5), or injected with vehicle (n = 5).
source: Mice were either fasted overnight (n = 5), fasted overnight and then refed 2 hr prior to euthanasia (n = 10), fed ad libitum (n = 5), injected with LiCl (n = 5), or injected with vehicle (n = 5).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.
